chunks: Drawing a boost converter circuit. The question: Draw a boost converter circuit.
To draw a boost converter, you put the inductor in series with the input, then hang a switch from the far end of the inductor down to ground.
From that same point, a diode leads to the output, where a capacitor and the load sit.
The key feature to get right is that the inductor sits on the input side, unlike in a buck converter.
Picture a road from the input on the left to the output on the right. The first thing on the road is the inductor. Just past it is a junction.
One branch is a trapdoor down to ground, which is the switch. The other branch has a one-way gate (the diode) leading to a tank (the capacitor) and the customers.
If you can trace the road and name each element, your drawing is correct.
The reference drawing. I L is the current in the inductor (always positive in CCM), and I D flows only when the switch is off.
The V out marker shows the output voltage is measured from the output node to ground. Check the diode symbol: the bar (cathode) is on the output side.
Switch node (SW): the junction between the inductor, switch, and diode. MOSFET: the transistor used as the switch.
A control signal on its gate (its control pin) turns it on and off. Schottky diode: a diode with a low forward voltage drop.
Feedback divider: two resistors that scale the output down for the controller ("Sensing buck output voltage and current").
Synchronous boost: a version where a second transistor replaces the diode.
The minimal drawing has five pieces. The input goes through the inductor to the switch node. The switch goes from the node to ground.
The diode goes from the node to the output, pointing toward the output: its anode (the end current enters) is on the node, its cathode on the output.
The capacitor goes from output to ground, and the load sits in parallel with it. For 3. 7 volts in and 5 volts out, the duty cycle is about 1-3. 7 over 5 equals 0. 26 .
That is the whole idea.
"Input on the left, inductor in series, then a switch node. From the switch node a MOSFET goes to ground, and a diode goes to the output with its anode on the switch node.
The output has a capacitor to ground and the load. So it's source, inductor, diode, output, with the switch pulling the middle node to ground.
I'd mark the switch node, the inductor current, the diode direction and ground, and mention the feedback divider and the sync-FET option."
